items.followUp: How is chemotherapy used to treat cancer?

rubric.why: Identifies the radiation or source used in radiotherapy.
rubric.description: Radiotherapy uses high-energy radiation, such as gamma rays from cobalt-60.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming radiation or a suitable radioactive source.

rubric.why: Explains how the treatment acts on cancer.
rubric.description: The radiation is directed at the cancer to destroy cancer cells or shrink the tumour.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the treatment’s effect on cancer cells or a tumour.

modelAnswer: Radiotherapy treats cancer by directing high-energy radiation, such as gamma rays from cobalt-60, at the cancerous area.
The radiation destroys cancer cells or shrinks the tumour.

items.followUp: State two properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Identifies one characteristic path of positive rays.
rubric.description: Positive rays travel in straight lines.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rays travel straight.

rubric.why: Identifies another characteristic of positive rays.
rubric.description: They are positively charged and are deflected towards the negative plate in an electric field.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct property distinct from straight-line travel.

modelAnswer: Positive rays travel in straight lines.
They are positively charged and are deflected towards the negative plate in an electric field.

items.followUp: How does atomic size change down a group, and how does this affect the ease of removing an outer electron?

rubric.why: States the direction of the ionization-energy trend.
rubric.description: Ionization energy generally decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct trend.

rubric.why: Explains why less energy is required to remove an electron down a group.
rubric.description: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is easier to remove.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid explanation involving increased distance or shielding and easier removal.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally decreases down a group.
Atomic size and shielding increase, so the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and easier to remove.

items.followUp: Why are the elements of the d-block shown in the main body of the periodic table?

rubric.why: Identifies the position or block of these elements.
rubric.description: Lanthanides and actinides are f-block elements belonging to periods 6 and 7, respectively.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying their f-block or period placement.

rubric.why: Explains why these series are displayed separately.
rubric.description: They are placed below the main table to keep the periodic table compact and not excessively wide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct layout reason.

modelAnswer: Lanthanides and actinides are f-block elements belonging to periods 6 and 7, respectively.
They are shown separately below the periodic table to keep it compact and avoid making it too wide.

items.followUp: Define a triple covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: States the number of electron pairs involved in a double covalent bond.
rubric.description: A double covalent bond forms when two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including two shared pairs.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a double bond.
rubric.description: An oxygen molecule (O₂) or a carbon–oxygen bond in carbon dioxide is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A double covalent bond is formed when two pairs of electrons are shared between two atoms.

items.followUp: What does δ− represent in a polar covalent bond, and how does it form?

rubric.why: Explains what the delta symbol denotes.
rubric.description: The delta sign (δ) indicates a partial charge, δ+ or δ−, on an atom in a polar covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as a partial charge.

rubric.why: Explains the origin of the partial charges.
rubric.description: A difference in electronegativity causes unequal sharing of electrons, producing partial charges.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking unequal electron sharing to electronegativity difference.

modelAnswer: The delta sign (δ) represents a partial charge: δ+ is partial positive and δ− is partial negative.
It develops in a polar covalent bond because atoms with different electronegativities share electrons unequally.

items.followUp: Define boiling point and condensation point.

rubric.why: Defines freezing point by the direction of the change of state.
rubric.description: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct liquid-to-solid definition.

rubric.why: Defines melting point by the direction of the change of state.
rubric.description: The melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct solid-to-liquid definition.

modelAnswer: Freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.
Melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid.

items.followUp: What is the transition temperature of sulfur, and which allotropes change at this temperature?

rubric.why: Defines transition temperature as a change between allotropes.
rubric.description: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: Gives a correct example of a transition temperature.
rubric.description: Sulfur changes from rhombic sulfur to monoclinic sulfur at about 96°C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct sulfur example and/or temperature.

modelAnswer: Transition temperature is the temperature at which one allotropic form changes into another.
For example, rhombic sulfur changes into monoclinic sulfur at about 96°C.
